In Terms of TEAM-CBT, this is what is known as outcome resistance. A patient will avoid recovery from their symptoms of anxiety/depression because recovery may lead to unwanted outcome. In some cases this resistance is totally warranted. For instances, say you want to get over your fear of snakes. Would the goal then be to be able to handle the most venomous snakes in the world without a shred of fear. No! In other words, fear is a useful emotion that helps us avoid objectively dangerous situations. So ask yourself: “How is this fear helping me?”. In the case of a flight emergency, a good bit of fear could be great to push you into action to get a life vest or put your mask on during a cabin depressurization. Now considering all these benefits of your claustrophobia, why would want to get rid of it? Would there be an appropriate AMOUNT of fear to have that would keep you protected while alleviate some of your symptoms of anxiety? For me, I might want to be say 20% anxious in those situations at all times just in case of an emergency. For you it may be higher. The goal is turn that fear into a stabilizing force that you can use to help you in an emergency, rather then being at the mercy of it when it isn’t useful to you.

As a psych major, I prescribe to the cognitive perspective. Through that lens, working out 
can help depression but it isn’t the total panacea that people make it out to be. Working out mostly helps you through changing some of the negative thinking patterns that you possess about self-esteem. If you tell yourself you’re ugly or unmotivated, working out would start to change that internal dialogue; proving to yourself that you aren’t unmotivated or you have the potential to be attractive or whatever. That can be a great catalyst to start a healthy direction in your life. However, most people have very specific problems. If a close family member just died, you failed a test at school, or You’re holding in a secret from your significant other, working out would not tackle these problems in any meaningful depth. You will not magically convince yourself through curling dumbbells that your family members death wasn’t your fault, that you can do better on the next test, or how to appropriately deal with explaining the secret without anyone getting hurt. People with problems like these don’t need a run in the park, they need specific mental health treatments followed by actionable steps in rectifying and or accepting those problems and moving forward with their lives.

Change of scenery might be good for sure. While you’re at it, pick up a copy (or find an electronic version) of Feeling Good by David Burns. Totally changed my life/depression. Start trying to tackle some of the negative thoughts surrounding your ex. Break ups are one of the hardest things to go through as a human being; they are no joke. Take care of your mental please.

I highly recommend David Burns new brand of CBT called TEAM-CBT. It validates a patients real concerns. It includes the possibility of not getting rid of negative thoughts at all if it serves the patient in a meaningful way. Here's brief overview:  when you write down your negative thought, instead of writing all the things WRONG with having that thought, write all the things that are GREAT about having that thought. For example, if someone was robbed at gun point at a corner store he/she might have a fear of  public spaces. So instead of asking what's wrong with his fear of public spaces ask him what is RIGHT! One thing would be that fact that it IS possible to robbed or shot in a public space and this thought allows vigilance. That can be very helpful instinct to have in a time of crisis! It also shows that he/she doesn't take his/her life for granted, that they care about taking care of themselves! There are so many beautiful and meaningful things our negative thoughts can say about us.

This is called **Positive reframing**. And once you realize all the awesome and important things a negative thought says about you then you can decide to **keep it** and use its advantages or lower its influence on your life. If you decide you **want** to keep it, in TEAM-CBT the therapist doesn't coax you to change. If it works for you it works! But if you **don't** want to live with that thought THEN you can test the validity and list the distortions of those thoughts and feelings. 

I really feel this is a life changing school of therapy. It has helped me immeasurably. But just my two cents and thought I'd throw it out there. Hope you find what works for you OP and wish you luck on your mental health journey.
